Niva Bupa Health Insurance, one of India’s leading standalone health insurers, is set to host the Niva Bupa Walk for Healthy Cities in New Delhi. Tennis icon and Olympic medallist Sania Mirza is coming to the capital this Sunday, September 27, to lead the Niva Bupa Walk for Healthy Cities, an initiative that brings together fitness, community and environmental action.The initiative aims to bring together citizens, fitness enthusiasts, families, corporate employees and community groups for a morning centred on walking, fitness and community engagement. The event is designed to encourage physical activity and healthier everyday habits while highlighting the connection between individual wellbeing and the health of the urban environment.Commenting on the initiative, Nimish Agrawal, Director, CMO & Head – Digital SBU, Niva Bupa Health Insurance , said, “Health is not just an individual pursuit; it is shaped by the environment and communities we live in. Through the Niva Bupa Walk for Healthy Cities, we want to make healthy living more participative, engaging and relevant to everyday life. Having Sania Mirza lead this initiative in Delhi adds an incredible energy to the movement and we hope her presence inspires more people to step out, move together and take small but meaningful steps towards healthier lives and healthier cities. ”The initiative brings together three simple ideas, move for your health, connect with your community and act for your environment, reinforcing the belief that small actions, when taken collectively, can create a larger impact.

Article Title: Who is Suruchi Singh? 19-year-old with 5 World Cup golds in one season goes from 26th in 10m air pistol individuals to Asian Games gold in mixed
Article Text:
Suruchi Singh, left, and Kamaljeet celebrate after winning Gold medal in the 10 meter air pistol mixed team final (PTI Photo)

From Jhajjar’s fields to the shooting range

The ritual before every big match

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Asian Games gold completes another breakthrough

Suruchi Singh and Kamaljeet won the maiden gold medal in shooting for India at the Asian Games 2026 after a stunning performance in the mixed team event.Kamaljeet and Suruchi shot a total of 484.6 in the final. They were followed by South Korea’s Suhyeon Hong and Gaeun Choo, who finished second with 478.0. The Korean pair were 6.6 points behind Kamaljeet and Suruchi, underlining the Indian duo’s dominance in the final.Iran bagged the bronze medal with 415.8.But Suruchi’s journey to the Asian Games gold medal was far from easy. The 19-year-old comes from a humble family in Haryana, and when TimesofIndia.com spoke to her coach Suresh Singh last year, he recalled how he agreed to train her, but only after laying down his own conditions.Born in Jhajjar, Haryana, Suruchi comes from a humble family. Her coach, Suresh Singh, has previously recalled how the youngster remains closely connected to her roots, helping with work at home and even operating farm machinery.“If she weren’t at the World Cup today, she’d be home harvesting wheat,” Suresh had told TOI.When Suruchi and her father, Inder Singh, first met the coach, her father made his priority clear: he wanted his daughter to learn discipline alongside the sport.Suresh agreed to take her on, but with a condition, Suruchi would have to follow his system rather than simply focus on pulling the trigger.That decision changed her career.Suruchi won medals at the 2022 and 2023 Nationals before producing a spectacular breakthrough in 2024, when she won seven gold medals at the National Championships in Delhi. She followed that up with two more gold medals at the National Games in Uttarakhand.In 2025, Suruchi began making headlines on the ISSF World Cup circuit, winning individual gold medals in Lima, Buenos Aires and Munich.Despite her international success, Suruchi has retained one habit that keeps her connected to the person who helped shape her career. Before a competition, she calls her coach. Even at major international events, she would contact Suresh minutes before stepping onto the range.“Sir, I have five minutes before I go in, what should I do?” she would ask.The Asian Games gold also reflected the mentality Suruchi has developed through years of training. If she decides to fire 150 shots during a training session and the final shot does not land where she wants it to, Suruchi does not simply pack up and leave. She keeps shooting until she gets the result she wants.The road to Friday’s gold had not been entirely smooth. Suruchi finished 26th in the women’s individual 10m air pistol qualification at the Asian Games, while India also missed out on a medal in the women’s team event.But the mixed team event offered another opportunity.Suruchi and Kamaljeet seized it. They topped the qualification before carrying that momentum into the final. Their 484.6 points gave them a clear advantage over South Korea and secured India’s maiden gold medal at the Asian Games 2026.
Article Summary: Suruchi singh and kamaljeet win maiden gold medal in shooting for india at the asian games 2026. The 19-year-old duo shot a total of 484.6 in the final. South korea’s suhyeon hong and gaeun choo, who finished second with 478.0, were 6.6 points behind.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: India one step away from defending kabaddi gold medals as men and women storm into finals
Article Text:
India's Men and Women's team reach final of the Asian Games 2026 (Agency Images)

India women overpower Nepal

Men produce another dominant performance

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India eye kabaddi double

India’s kabaddi team continued their dominance at the Asian Games 2026 as both the men’s and women’s teams secured their places in the gold-medal matches with semifinal victories. The women’s side defeated Nepal 48-24, while the men’s team followed with an emphatic 66-27 win over Thailand. The results ensured that India will have a chance to defend both kabaddi titles at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.For the women, the victory kept alive their bid for a fourth consecutive Asian Games gold medal. India have won the women’s kabaddi title at every Asian Games since the sport was introduced to the women’s programme in 2010.The Indian women established control early and went into the interval with a 31-17 advantage. India combined successful raids with a disciplined defensive effort and repeatedly put Nepal under pressure. The four all-outs in the opening half gave the defending champions a substantial cushion.Nepal struggled to match India's intensity after the break. They managed only seven points in the second half as India maintained their advantage and eventually completed a 24-point victory.The win extended India's unbeaten run in the competition. They had previously defeated Iran, Bangladesh and Japan during the group stage. The defending champions will now turn their attention to the final, where they will look to maintain their remarkable record in the women's event.The men's team delivered an equally commanding performance against Thailand. India raced into an early lead and were comfortably ahead at 37-18 at half-time. Thailand showed flashes of resistance, with Theeradat Chaisit producing a strong spell in attack, but India quickly regained control.The Indian side continued to pile on the points after the break and eventually crossed the 50-point mark. Thailand could not keep pace with India's raiders and defenders as the gap continued to widen. India eventually closed out the semifinal with a 66-27 victory.The two semifinal victories mean India are now guaranteed medals in both kabaddi competitions. The women's team are chasing a fourth successive gold, while the men are aiming to retain the title they won at the previous Asian Games.India have historically dominated men's kabaddi at the Asian Games, having won eight gold medals since the sport made its debut in 1990. Iran are the only other nation to have won the men's title, doing so in 2018 when India had to settle for bronze.The Indian teams will now have one final hurdle to clear in Nagoya.
Article Summary: India's men and women's kabaddi teams reach final of the asian games 2026. The women's side defeated nepal 48-24, while the men's team followed with an emphatic 66-27 win over thailand. The two semifinal victories mean india are now guaranteed medals in both competitions. India are chasing a fourth successive gold in the women's event.

Article Title: 'Final mein gai, to gold hi layegi': Suruchi Inder Singh's coach after Asian Games 2026 triumph
Article Text:
Suruchi and her teammate Kamaljeet won gold in the 10m air pistol mixed team event (Image credit: Agencies)

Suruchi's gold-winning show

Hours of work before the Asian Games

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: “Final mein gayi, to gold hi layegi,” an elated Suresh Singh said after his student Suruchi Inder Singh helped India win its first gold medal of the day at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Friday.Suruchi and her teammate Kamaljeet won gold in the 10m air pistol mixed team event, finishing on top at the Aichi General Shooting Range to give India its second gold medal of the Games.For Suruchi, the victory came after a disappointing individual event.The Haryana shooter, who won four individual World Cup gold medals in 2025 in Buenos Aires, Munich, Lima and Doha, including the World Cup Final, failed to qualify for the final in the individual 10m air pistol event. In a field of 55 shooters, she finished 26th in qualification with a score of 568-12x.“She was disappointed. But I knew she would come back stronger. She knows how to bounce back quickly, and that is her best quality. The moment she reached the final, I was 200 percent sure that she would win gold. That’s how she is,” the coach said.Suruchi and Kamaljeet were in control from the start of the mixed team final. The pair scored 103.0 in the first series of Stage 1, followed by 202.4 and 303.5.They continued their strong performance in Stage 2, scoring 364.7 in the first series and staying comfortably ahead of South Korea and Iran.After 18 shots, India remained at the top and extended their lead with a score of 424.9 in the second series of Stage 2.Suruchi and Kamaljeet eventually finished with a total score of 484.6 to win the gold medal.South Korea's Suhyeon Hong and Gaeun Choo finished second with 478.0. The Korean pair were 6.6 points behind the Indians, underlining India's control of the final.“She is an athlete for the finals. Look at her past record. If she has reached the final, then you can't stop her. She will go for gold. She doesn't want silver or bronze. She has that kind of hunger,” Suresh said.Ahead of the Asian Games, Suruchi worked on several aspects of her shooting with Suresh at his Guru Dronacharya Shooting Academy in Bhiwani.The coach said they focused on her technique, holding and dry-fire training. Suruchi's father had initially wanted her to take up wrestling.“She worked on her holding and did dry-fire training for hours to improve her focus. We also worked on some technical aspects,” he said.One of the key areas they focused on was timing.“The most important focus was on timing. I am a coach who focuses on timing and wants my shooter to finish the match early. I told the same thing to Suruchi. We used to decide a particular time and try to finish the shot within that time.“For example, if you have 60 seconds for one shot, finish that shot early. It helps you take the pressure off yourself and allows you to focus,” he said.Now, Suresh is waiting to welcome his student home.“I am just waiting for her. She has made everyone proud. We are eagerly waiting to welcome her,” the coach said.
Article Summary: Suruchi inder singh helped india win its first gold medal of the day at the asian games 2026 in aichi-nagoya, japan. Suruchi and her teammate kamaljeet won gold in the 10m air pistol mixed team event. The victory came after a disappointing individual event.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge
Article Text:
El Rubius reacted honestly after his elimination from MrBeast’s $1 million challenge, calling it “unfair” and claiming he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings. His response felt real and balanced, especially after MrBeast’s team later sent him a cake, softening the moment.

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeast’s $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a raw reaction with fans, giving them a closer look at what the experience felt like from inside the game. It was not polished or carefully framed. It felt real, and that is exactly why it caught attention so quickly.The clip and his response have since fueled conversations across the streaming space. Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.Speaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which I’ve already distributed. It went to the mods, the subs, and the non-subs alike."He further added, "I’m happy, of course, though admittedly, it was incredibly tough.I wasn't really a fan of the challenge itself, either. But then again... it was basically a three-against-one situation the entire time. I mean, they were targeting me specifically the whole way through. I kept trying to go after RaKai, but, well, he actually just got eliminated in the end. So, at least justice was served for Abraham. Abraham, if you’re watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. Seriously, thank you for all the support and for just being there."He added, "Every time I asked for something in the chat or whatever it was, you guys were right there. You’re incredible. I’m a little disappointed in myself, personally, mostly for not performing better, but hey, I gave it my all, and we still walked away with $50,000, so we’ve got to look on the bright side. All right, guys, big hugs to all my brothers out there!"Interestingly, the story did not end with frustration. Later that day, Rubius revealed that MrBeast’s team had sent him a cake after his exit. It was a small gesture, but it shifted the mood. It showed that even in a high-pressure challenge, there is still room for respect.In the end, Rubius’ reaction felt honest and grounded. That is what stayed with people.
Article Summary: El rubius was eliminated from mrbeast's $1 million challenge. He called it "unfair" and said he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings.

Article Title: ​At 90, former paratrooper Ian Winship runs 10K in about an hour with daughter and grandson, setting a world-best time for his age
Article Text:
Pic credit: Gibson Digital/North Lanarkshire Council

Age, just a number

Pic credit: Gibson Digital/North Lanarkshire Council

3 generations in motion

Pic credit: Gibson Digital/North Lanarkshire Council

Ian Winship, a 90-year-old runner from North Lanarkshire, has completed a 10-kilometre race in about 1 hour, 4 minutes and 37 seconds, setting what is believed to be a world-best time for his age group. On 13 September, the former paratrooper completed the Cumbernauld 10K run. "I stood greetin'," the former paratrooper told the BBC, his disbelief still evident.It's easy to understand why. Winship wasn't chasing records when he started that morning. He was doing what he does most days: running. The world-best time in the M90 category came out of the blue. “It's just unbelievable. Cumbernauld might be famous now because of me.”Scottish Athletics confirmed the achievement is considered a ‘world best’ rather than a ‘world record’, as non-professional road races lack the precision required for official ratification. But there are simply no reports of anyone older achieving a faster time.Ian Winship, who hails from Cumberland, revealed the secret behind the record. He gets up each morning, fetches his paper, gets his coffee, and walks.Not around the block, but for miles. Most days, he hits 20,000 steps. Long stretches through Cumbernauld are a regimen he religiously follows to keep himself fit.Winship understands what most people don’t. “I've got a purpose, I want to stay alive. If I sit in the house I'll vegetate. I must meet people.” So he walks and continues to share ties with the community. It’s the perspective of someone who spent his younger years as a paratrooper, jumping into Egypt near Port Said during the Suez Crisis in 1956, and later became a steeplejack. Motion was always the job. Now it's the medicine.For him, what really works is consistency. He does not have a fancy training plan or gym membership. But every morning he wakes up and gets moving. His next challenge is to ‘live to 100’.When Winship completed the race, he was a little ‘wobbly’, so the paramedics offered him a wheelchair. But the 90-year-old turned it down immediately.Winship had the best company in the race. The nonagenarian ran this race alongside his daughter, Fiona Fleming, and grandson Kyle Fleming, 26, who came third. It wasn't their first time making the race a family affair at Cumbernauld. But the grandfather's performance still caught them off guard.Kyle is proud of his grandpa. “He gets up every morning, goes to get his paper, goes to get his coffee. He does 20,000 steps a day. It's incredible,” he told the broadcaster."I run because it keeps me sane, keeps me fit and it keeps me out of trouble,” Winship always told his family.For Kyle, watching his grandpa was inspiration enough. "That's always stuck with me. Every time I see him running, that's what I think about. He lost his wife years ago, and I think it just keeps him going."Meanwhile, Scottish Athletics said Winship's achievement is considered a ‘world best’ in the M90 category. A spokesperson for the body said they were "delighted to hear of Ian's great run". "Athletics can be for life if that's what you want and performances like this one by Ian at 90 really are inspirational."Kenneth Duffy, provost of North Lanarkshire, called him ‘a hero’. "My huge congratulations to Ian on his outstanding achievement at this year's Cumbernauld 10K event. What a hero he is! I'm sure everyone will be inspired by his determination, commitment and enthusiasm. To complete a 10K at 90 years of age is a remarkable accomplishment, let alone complete it in such an impressive time."Geraldine Woods, convener of communities at the council, also lauded Winship’s achievement. "Ian's performance at this year's event, along with his dedication and positive attitude, is an inspiration to people of all ages."
Article Summary: Ian winship, a 90-year-old runner from north lanarkshire, has completed a 10-kilometre race in about 1 hour, 4 minutes and 37 seconds. The former paratrooper completed the cumbernauld 10k run on 13 september. Scottish athletics said winship's achievement is considered a 'world best' in the m90 category.

Article Title: BGMI Gully Wars announced: Registration deadline, qualifier dates and prize pool
Article Text:
BGMI Gully Wars is here

BGMI Gully Wars qualifiers begin October 14, with 16 teams set to reach the finals

Krafton India has announced BGMI Gully Wars, a new open-for-all Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI) tournament with a prize pool of Rs 10 lakh. Registrations are live now and will close on October 6. There is no entry barrier for prior competitive experience, so any squad can sign up.The idea is to find players who are good but largely unknown. Many BGMI players are known only within their own squads, college groups or local Discord servers, and rarely get a proper shot at organised play. Gully Wars, which runs on the tagline "Apna Naam Bana", is pitched as that first step. The tournament is being organised in partnership with JioBLAST.The competition opens with an In-Game Qualifier running from October 14 to 20. Teams that make it through will move into a series of elimination rounds, which cut the field down to the final 16 teams for the Grand Finals. Dates for the later stages and the prize split have not been detailed yet.Karan Pathak, Associate Director - Esports, Krafton India, said the tournament is aimed at the next generation of competitive players."We look forward to seeing players from across the country step up, make their mark and, most importantly, make their name," he said.To register, players need to visit kraftonindiaesports.com and click the BGMI Gully Wars banner, or head to the Tournaments section and select "Register Now". First-time users will have to create an account, while existing users can log in with their credentials or through OTP verification. Tournament updates and announcements will be shared on the Krafton India Esports and JioBLAST Instagram handles.For squads that have so far only tested themselves in custom rooms with friends, this is a straightforward way to see how they stack up nationally. The deadline to get in is October 6.
Article Summary: Bgmi gully wars is a new open-for-all battlegrounds mobile india (bgmi) tournament. There is no entry barrier for prior competitive experience, so any squad can sign up. The competition opens with an in-game qualifier running from october 14 to 20.

Article Title: Nike Alphafly 4 launched with lighter ZoomX LT foam and 10% more energy return
Article Text:
Nike Alphafly 4 are 5% lighter than Alphafly 3

Two foams now sandwich the plate

The upper is designed for tired feet

Nike has launched the Alphafly 4, the newest version of its marathon racing shoe, with changes to nearly every major part. The company says it returns 10% more energy than its predecessor and weighs 5% less in a men's size 8.5.The biggest change is in the midsole. Nike has added a new ZoomX LT foam, which it says is up to 17% lighter than standard ZoomX and offers 8% more energy return. The shoe goes on early, limited sale on nike.com from today, September 17, with wider availability on nike.com and at select stores from October 29.ZoomX LT doesn't fully replace regular ZoomX. Nike layers the two foams above and below the carbon-fibre Flyplate, which keeps the Alphafly's signature propulsive scoop. The plate adds stability and guides a smooth forward roll, which should help runners hold a steady cadence. Up front, dual Air Zoom units have been retuned to work alongside the foam and plate at push-off. A lightweight Fast Shot outsole handles grip.The new Atomknit upper is seamless and breathable. It uses zoned midfoot cables, an integrated heel unit and a molded sock liner to hold the foot securely over long distances.Nike says development drew on athlete feedback across Alphafly generations, learnings from Project Dreamweaver, and extensive women's trials. Emily Farina, Senior Principal, Running Footwear, Nike Sport Research Lab, said the team studied how fatigue changes running mechanics."Our goal was simple: create a shoe that helps athletes feel more confident and capable deep into the race," she said.Nike athlete Addisu Gobena has already tested that claim. He wore the Alphafly 4 to a course-record marathon win in Sydney, and said he trusted the shoe when the race got difficult.
Article Summary: Nike alphafly 4 is the newest version of its marathon racing shoe. The company says it returns 10% more energy than its predecessor and weighs 5% less in a men's size 8.5. Nike has added a new zoomx lt foam, which it says is up to 17% lighter than standard zoomx.

Article Title: '15 years ... I waited for long': Krishna Jaisankar set for her India moment at Asian Games
Article Text:
Krishna Jaisankar (Image credit: Agencies)

A long road to the India jersey

Paris 2024 became a turning point

From a basketball family to shot put

Chasing Asian Games glory

Olympics - the ultimate dream

The chase for 18 metres

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of Krishna journey do you find most inspiring? Her long wait for recognition Her ability to overcome injuries Her confidence in her body Her dedication to the sport 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

'Dreams do come true'

Whenever Krishna Jaisankar gets some time, she opens her kit bag and looks at the badge on her T-shirt.It has one word written on it: INDIA.Every time she looks at it, her eyes get moist. But there is also a sense of confidence that builds within her. After waiting for 15 years, Krishna knows that when she finally wears the India jersey in Japan, it will mean much more than simply making her Asian Games debut.For the 23-year-old shot putter, the jersey will represent 15 years of ups and downs, missed opportunities, injuries and countless moments when she had to pick herself up and start again.“It's a surreal feeling. I just can't wait to don that jersey in Japan. 15 years.... I waited for long and yes, I have earned it. I am very appreciative, like I'm very grateful for the opportunity and to be able to finally put Team India on my back,” Krishna told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.After missing out on selection several times, Krishna finally broke through and earned her place in the Indian team for the Asian Games 2026.Now, as she prepares to travel to Japan, the Indian shot putter wants to leave the old disappointments behind and write a new chapter - one that she hopes will end with a medal.Her message to herself when she reaches Japan is simple.“All right, it's showtime,” Krishna said.Krishna's journey has never been an easy one. There were moments when she wanted to give up. She left India at a young age, first moving to Jamaica and later to the United States, as she looked for opportunities to develop as an athlete.Then came the Commonwealth Games opportunity. Krishna was among the favourites to make it to the big event, but a hamstring injury disrupted her plans.She tore her hamstring just three weeks before the event. Yet, she returned to competition and managed to qualify for the Asian Games. She also became the national champion after 15 years.“I just think the fighter mentality that I have. Never to give up. Never to settle. Setbacks are meant for something. Setbacks are supposed to mould you, but not define you,” she said.The biggest setback came in 2024. Marred by injuries, Krishna missed the Paris Olympics. But the difficult phase also forced her to look closely at herself and rethink the way she was approaching her career.She began paying more attention to her nutrition, sleep and recovery. She also started spending more time reflecting and talking to herself.“It was a very rough period for me,” she said.“I left my country, left my family, left my comfort zone. What does my opportunity cost? What am I getting back? I'm not making the team, I'm not competing. Why am I getting injured?” she said.That period eventually changed her approach towards her ultimate goal - representing India.Instead of looking too far ahead, Krishna decided to take things one step at a time.“If you've got a dream, you've got to protect it. You have a dream, you've got to protect it,” Krishna said.Krishna grew up in a sporting family. Her parents, Prasanna and Jay Shankar, have been involved in basketball, and she closely watched the work they put into developing the sport. Her mother has also been a national selector for Indian basketball.But Krishna eventually chose athletics and found her own identity in shot put.“I think my inspiration was within my corners, which is my family. Whatever I am today it is because of their support. I wanted to choose a different sport and I did and I am really happy about it,” she said.“Thanks to the Reliance Foundation, the Athletics Federation of India, the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu, and everyone in Tamil Nadu. Everybody has supported me and believed in me,” the 23-year-old said.Making her Team India debut at the Asian Games is a special moment for Krishna. But she does not want the excitement of finally making the team to overshadow her bigger target - winning a medal.Once she is in Japan, she wants to treat the competition like any other championship.“Now it's go time, there is no look back. I am looking forward, looking ahead in the future,” she said.“It's going to be a show, man. It's going to be a show from all sectors of athletics. Let it be track, let it be field, we're going to put up a show. All we ask in return, support us. Keep us in your prayers,” Krishan said.For Krishna, the Asian Games is not the end goal. It is a start. Her bigger dream is the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.She carries an Olympic chain with her even though she is yet to compete at the Games. For her, it is a reminder of where she wants to go.“I'm not an Olympian, but every single day I aspire to be one. I'm confident now I can say that that dream is no longer a dream. It's like, I'm converting it to be a reality,” she said.Krishna won a gold medal at the National Federation Cup 2026 and, in the process, broke her own record of 17.09m. She won the top prize with a personal best throw of 17.35m.Now, Krishna has set herself the target of crossing 18 metres. She believes the Asian Games 2026 will be a great platform to achieve that feat while also challenging for the gold medal.“I am getting closer,” she said. “But again, it's very important to believe in the process. No better place to do it than Japan. Let's have a PB in Japan. I know I am a medal contender,” she said. “So, the mindset also is walking into the thing and be like, you know what, I'm walking in as a medal contender, not as a participant,” she said.Bodyshaming: Turning comments into strengthKrishna has been muscular since childhood. Her appearance sometimes made her uncomfortable. She felt that she did not fit what she believed was society's traditional idea of how a woman should look.“I didn't even know the meaning of body shaming until, you know, somebody came and told me, hey, somebody's body shaming you,” she said.But over the years, Krishna learned to see her body differently. The same body that some people made fun of became the body that helped her break records and earn her place in Team India.“To show the world, to show the society, that the body that you're making fun of and making me feel that I'm ashamed of is the body that's helping me break records, is the body that's helping me debut for Team India at the Asian Games,” she said.Her message to young girls is direct.“Be confident in who you are. Do not change yourself for somebody. She also has another message: do not live for other people's approval. Do not seek validation from people because again, comparison is a thief of joy,” she said.With 15 years of pain now behind her, Krishna is ready to write a new chapter in Japan. When she steps into the throwing circle with the shot in her hand, the 23-year-old will perhaps remember the 18-year-old version of herself who first dared to dream of representing India.Asked what she would say to the 18-year-old Krishna, the 23-year-old replied: “Dreams do come true”.“Know that your story is not just your journey. It's a story of so many untold stories. There are so many people that look up to you. If you have a dream, you bloody protect it,” Krishna signed off.
Article Summary: Krishna jaisankar will make her asian games debut at the 2026 event. The 23-year-old shot putter has waited 15 years for her chance to represent india. She has overcome injuries and missed opportunities on her way to japan. Krishna is set to make her team india debut at the asian games 2026.

Article Title: 'He was abusing him nonstop': Dhruv Jurel reveals what triggered Yashavi Jaiswal’s clash with Asitha Fernando
Article Text:
Jurel reveals Jaiswal Fernando confrontation (Image: IANS)

'He didn't say anything'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

‘He never starts it’

The on-field confrontation between India opener Yashasvi Jaiswal and Sri Lanka pacer Asitha Fernando during the second Test in Colombo had become one of the talking points of the series. Nearly a month after the incident, India wicketkeeper-batter Dhruv Jurel has revealed what Jaiswal told him about the exchange.The incident took place during the opening session on Day 1 of the second Test. Jaiswal was batting aggressively on 45 and had already struck Fernando for three boundaries in the over before the Sri Lankan pacer dismissed him with the final delivery of the 17th over.Fernando celebrated the wicket with an animated send-off as Jaiswal began walking back towards the dressing room. However, the Indian batter soon turned around and walked back towards the Sri Lankan pacer, leading to a heated confrontation.The two players came face-to-face before teammates and the Sri Lankan captain intervened to separate them. Jurel has now claimed that Jaiswal told him Fernando had been verbally abusing him continuously following the dismissal.“When he got out, he was quietly walking back to the dressing room. He didn't say anything. If you look at the footage, Jaiswal immediately turned around. The Sri Lankan pacer was abusing him.Jaiswal told me that he was abusing him nonstop,” Jurel told former India batter Aakash Chopra.According to Jurel, Jaiswal did not object to Fernando celebrating the wicket but drew the line at personal abuse.“Jaiswal told him, ‘It's okay. You took my wicket, you can show normal aggression, but you can't abuse me,’” Jurel added.Jurel, who is also Jaiswal's teammate at Rajasthan Royals , described the opener as someone who does not generally initiate verbal exchanges but is willing to respond when provoked.When Chopra suggested that Jaiswal is a “feisty guy” who gives it back when someone provokes him, Jurel agreed.“100 per cent. He will never start it; I have never seen him do that. He is always in the zone; he is always thinking about his batting. But if you provoke us, we will also return it,” Jurel said.The confrontation eventually required the intervention of players from both sides, bringing an end to the tense exchange on the field. Both Jaiswal and Fernando were subsequently sanctioned by the International Cricket Council for breaches of its Code of Conduct following the incident.
Article Summary: India wicketkeeper-batter dhruv jurel reveals what jaiswal told him about the confrontation. The incident took place during the opening session on day 1 of the second test in colombo. The sri lankan pacer asitha fernando celebrated the wicket with an animated send-off.

Article Title: Asian Games: Joshna Chinappa makes history with sixth medal; Anahat, Abhay storm into semis as India assure three squash medals
Article Text:
Anahat Singh and Joshna Chinappa (PTI/ANI Photos)

Joshna seals sixth Asian Games medal

Anahat, Abhay march into singles semifinals

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India assured themselves of three squash medals at the Asian Games 2026 on Friday as Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar entered the mixed doubles semifinals, while Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh advanced to the last four in the women’s and men’s singles respectively.For Joshna, the semifinal berth carried added significance. The 40-year-old, competing at her record seventh Asian Games, secured her sixth medal at the continental showpiece with Senthilkumar. The Indian duo produced a dominant 11-3, 11-5 win over the Philippines’ David Pelino and Jemyca Aribado in their quarterfinal.Junior world champion Anahat and Abhay also continued their campaigns with straight-game victories, leaving India with three medal assurances across the squash events.Joshna and Senthilkumar needed less than half an hour to dispatch the Philippine pair at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena. The Indians took control from the start, racing to a 3-0 lead and quickly extending it to 9-2 before wrapping up the opening game 11-3 in nine minutes.The second game was more competitive initially, with Pelino and Aribado reducing the deficit to 4-2. But Joshna and Senthilkumar shifted gears again, moving to 7-2 and then 8-4 before closing out the match 11-5.They will face Hong Kong’s Yo Ka Lee and Ming Hong Tang in Saturday’s semifinal.“Winning a medal for your country is always very special. And that's been my motivation all my career,” Joshna told PTI after the match.The medal will take Joshna’s Asian Games tally to six, including two silver. Her previous medals include a singles bronze in 2018, team silver in 2014 and 2018, and team bronze in 2010 and 2022.Joshna has now surpassed Saurav Ghosal’s record of six Asian Games appearances, having competed at every edition since the 2002 Busan Games.Anahat continued her impressive campaign with a commanding 11-2, 11-5, 11-3 victory over compatriot Tanvi Khanna in the women’s singles quarterfinal.The junior world champion and medal favourite will now look to take another step towards the gold medal and a potential Olympic qualification. The singles gold medallists at the Asian Games will directly qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its Olympic debut.In the men’s singles, Abhay overcame local favourite Ryonosuke Tsukue 11-4, 11-3, 11-6 to book his place in the last four.He will face Pakistan’s Irfan Muhammad, who defeated India’s Veer Chotrani 6-11, 11-8, 11-3, 11-3 in 41 minutes after recovering from a game down.
Article Summary: Joshna chinappa and velavan senthilkumar into mixed doubles semifinals. Anahat singh and abhay singh advance to last four in women's and men's singles. India assured themselves of three squash medals at the asian games 2026.

Article Title: From Russia to India: Meet Yury Lisichko, the man fixing shooters' pistol grips
Article Text:
Yury Lisichko (Image credit: TimesofIndia.com)

Yury Lisichko (Image credit: Timesofindia.com)

Yury Lisichko (Image credit: TimesofIndia.com)

The 200-page CV that brought him to India

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

How the coach became the man shooters call for grips

Yury Lisichko (Image credit: TimesofIndia.com)

NEW DELHI: There are tools on the table, pieces of wood on the floor, and pistol grips in various stages of modification. Some tools hang around the room. His T-shirt and eyelashes are covered with wooden husk. A few used coffee mugs are lying around.Two cats wander in and out.This is Yury Lisichko's workshop in Greater Noida, where Indian shooters arrive with a problem that can be difficult to explain and even harder to fix: the grip of their pistol does not feel right.Lisichko looks at the weapon, studies the shooter's hand and wrist, examines the existing grip and starts working on it. The shooter then takes the pistol into another room and aims at a target.A few shots are followed by more adjustments, and then more shot follow. The process continues until Lisichko is satisfied with the grip and the shooter is comfortable with it."I know the mentality of every shooter. I speak to them for one or two minutes... that's it. I get the problem. Now, I tell them to be seated until I am done. They wait, I work and when I am ready I give them targets to shoot. First, I need to be satisfied and then them.I make grips with a fresh piece of wood. I don't use old wood or just paste and give them. I want these shooters to do well," Lisichko told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.Shooters have been coming to him for years. Anish Bhanwala, Jitu Rai, Manu Bhaker and Sarabjot Singh are among those he has worked with. juniors, seniors, and international shooters all come, even during major competitions, and the door remains open."Anish [Bhanwala] came to me just ahead of the Asian Games. He spent the entire day here. When the solution didn't come, he decided to stay here to avoid much travel. Many Commonwealth Games and Asian Games shooters came to me. Shooters come here, stay too. They order their food and play with my cats. All I tell them is, 'Don't disturb me,'" Lisichko said.However, Lisichko did not come to India to become a grip specialist. He arrived in 2009 as a foreign pistol shooting coach.In 2007, Lisichko was involved with the European Championships in St Petersburg. After the competition, foreign coaches asked him why they had never seen him work abroad with athletes.He decided to put together a CV, that too a 200-page one containing his education, the athletes he had worked with in Russia, his achievements and other details of his career.Two years later, he got a call from India."That was the first time when I heard Indian English. It's absolutely not understandable. I remember that conversation. I could not understand the accent much. He disconnected the call saying, 'Call me later with someone who speaks good English, please," Lisichko recalled.The Indian Army wanted him to work in India. At the Indian embassy, he was shown an order from the Defence Ministry concerning the appointment of foreign coaches for the Army.He said yes. His visa was ready the next day and Lisichko landed in New Delhi, travelled to Indore and then reached Mhow - a cantonment town in Indore, Madhya Pradesh."I had no knowledge about India. I knew this was a country with a lot of wild animals and snakes everywhere, spiders everywhere. But with time, I realised it is beautiful. I have travelled around India and met different people. Everyone is different," he said.He started working with Army shooters, including at the Infantry School in Mhow and the Army Marksmanship Unit. He also worked with India's junior pistol shooting setup and later with senior athletes.For the first three or four months, the accent, more than the language was a problem. Slowly, he began speaking in a similar way. Then came Hindi, Indian food, and the small exchanges that came with everyday life in the country."Namaste. Namaskaar. Kaise ho. Theek ho. Kaha jaa rahe ho. When I go to the market, I have learnt to say, 'Kitna hua bhaiya? Mere paise wapas do.' I have learnt that Hindi is a very simple language. And it's so far from techniques. It seems like the Ukrainian language. Because I am ethnically Ukrainian. But you see, my heart is with Ukraine, my brain is partly in Russia," Lisichko said.Lisichko had studied technology at Moscow Aviation University and had experience working with wood and other materials. His work with pistol grips developed gradually.The first attempts did not go smoothly. "The first grip was destroyed, the second grip was destroyed. After that I made a grip with which I started to work. And began to improve my level in shooting. With time I excelled in the art of making grips," he recalled.That work eventually became a specialised part of what he does for shooters."I didn't know the study in woods, experience would become a specialised craft and I will be now helping shooters in fixing grips ahead of competitions. When they win, I silently pat on my back too (laugh)," Lisichko said.There is no standard grip that can simply be transferred from one shooter to another. The same pistol can feel different in different hands."You can buy the same rifle as Abhinav Bindra. You can buy the same pistol as Manu Bhaker or Jitu Rai or Vijay Kumar. You can buy a shooting suit the same as Bindra. Shooting boots like Bindra. You can use the same pellets, the same gloves, everything. But you can't shoot with the same grip. Every human hand and the ability to hold something are different. So grip is something that makes a shooter uncomfortable and destroys their focus," he said.That is why the pistol sometimes arrives at Lisichko's workshop before it reaches the competition range. The shooter has to wait as he works on the wood, and then comes another set of shots and recalibration.
Article Summary: Yury lisichko is a russian pistol shooting coach in greater noida, india. He has been working with indian shooters since 2009. His 200-page cv includes his education, achievements and other details of his career. Lisichko had studied technology at moscow aviation university and had experience working with wood and other materials.

Article Title: Her mother thought she was in Bengaluru. Seema Kumari was actually winning Asian Games bronze in Nagoya
Article Text:
Seema (Image credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

On Thursday night, when a beaming Seema Kumari took a short lap of honour draped in the tricolour, congratulatory messages began pouring in. It was perhaps then that her mother realised her daughter was in Nagoya and not Bengaluru.Seema’s 75-year-old mother, who lives in Reta in Himachal Pradesh, suffers from hypertension. Concerned about her daughter’s well-being, she is often kept in the dark about Seema’s travels and competitions.But after the stupendous performance Seema delivered on a windy night at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, her mother will have plenty to celebrate. So will a nation, after the 25-year-old opened India’s athletics medal account with a bronze in the women’s 10,000m.In a tight race, Seema clocked 32:50.05 to finish behind Bahrain’s Winfred Yavi (32:39.18) and Japan’s Nozomi Tanaka (32:41.54).Her bronze ended India’s 16-year wait for a medal in the event at the Asian Games. Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut had won gold and silver respectively, at the 2010 Games.It was a race built on endurance, pace, persistence and planning. Up against a star-studded field, Seema could have been forgiven for feeling the pressure.Instead, she focused on the distance rather than the runners around her.Her consistency was remarkable. Across all 25 laps, she never fell out of the leading pack. With two laps to go, she even raised hopes of a silver, but Bahrain’s Yavi stepped on the gas at the 200m mark and Tanaka accelerated, leaving Seema to settle for bronze.For Seema, who lost her father at a young age and is one of six siblings, it was a special medal on her Asian Games debut.“The race was very tactical. Everyone ran for the medal and I also thought that I would fight for it. Although I’m happy that I’ve earned a medal in my first Asian Games, I hope to change the colour of the medal in the 5000 metres event.”The past year-and-a-half has seen Seema on a rising curve training under coach Scott Simmons.“I’ve been training with Simmons for the past three years and have been sent to the USA for camps and training. It is very beneficial because conditions are tough there and we train with Olympic champions,” she said. Seema won a silver at the World University Games last year.As expected, India’s medal of the day came from the 4x400m mixed relay team. In a thrilling comeback, the quartet of Manu Saji, MR Poovamma, Vishal TK and Vithya Ramraj clocked 3:14.46 to take silver behind Bahrain, who won gold in a Games-record timing of 3:12.87.India did not have the best of starts, with Manu unable to provide the initial momentum. Poovamma, however, hauled the team back into contention with a strong second leg.Vishal then closed the gap and put India firmly in medal bracket before Vithya produced an impressive anchor leg. With the Vietnam runner breathing down her neck, she held her nerve in the home straight to fend off the challenge. The Vietnamese quartet finished just 0.08 seconds behind with 3:14.54.Jay Kumar and Kiran Phal, who ran the morning heats, were replaced with Vishal and Vithya for the final.Asha Ilango narrowly missed out on a triple jump medal, finishing fourth behind China’s Li Yi on countback after both athletes recorded a best jump of 13.83m. Asha needed to better 13.79m with her final attempt to move ahead of Li, but could manage only 13.59m. The other Indian in the fray, Niharika Vashisht, finished 10th.Gurindervir Singh eased into the 100m semifinals. He clocked 10.38 seconds to finish second in Heat 4. Animesh Kujur also qualified for the 100m semifinals.
Article Summary: Seema kumari won bronze in the women's 10,000m. Her bronze ended india’s 16-year wait for a medal in the event at the asian games. The 25-year-old won a silver at the world university games last year. He clocked 10.38 seconds to finish second in heat 4. Animesh kujur also qualified for the 100m semifinals.
